newsitem.title: USA: Bond mkt view on rates unchanged by Greenspan talk.
newsitem.headline: Bond mkt view on rates unchanged by Greenspan talk.

text.p: U.S. bond market analysts continued to expect that the Federal Reserve's next move on monetary policy will be a tightening, although they said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan on Tuesday did quell fears that the Fed would raise rates in the next few weeks.

"Greenspan is much closer to accepting the case for a tightening than he ever was last year, but he has not yet finally made up his mind," concluded Ian Shepherdson, chief U.S. economist at HSBC Capital Markets, noting the Fed chief's concern over higher wages.

Other analysts agreed that Greenspan's testimony before the U.S. Senate Budget Committee did nothing to change the views they held before he spoke. Some expect a rate hike as early as the first quarter of 1997, others as late as 1998.

Without a clear signal on interest rates, it took a while for the market to decide which way to move after Greenspan spoke. Treasury prices fell on initial reports of Greenspan's prepared testiomy. But as his remarks eventually calmed the market, prices rebounded. The 30-year bond ended New York trading Tuesday up about a half-point to yield 6.79 percent amid relief that Greenspan was less hawkish than expected.

"Prior to his testimony, every foreign and domestic account was building in a worst-case scenario," noted Brett Benza, senior trader at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "But he didn't seem to say anything that would destroy the market."
The last time Greenspan spoke in the U.S. on December 5, he spooked financial markets -- both foreign and domestic -- by wondering aloud whether asset prices were too high.

Since then, bond yields have jumped nearly a half-point, as economic data the past month was on the strong side. So, it was no surprise the market expected the worst from Greenspan in his latest remarks.
Instead, Greenspan spoke of a robust economy, with few signs of inflation, although he warned that wage pressures could pose a problem in the future.

"The economy has retained considerable vigor, with few signs of the imbalances and inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions," he said. "The important question from a monetary policy point-of-view is whether labor market conditions will be consistent with the maintenance of satisfactory (consumer) price performance."

Greenspan's remarks seemed to echo those of other Fed officials, mainly Fed Governors Laurence Meyer and Susan Phillips, from last week, players said. Accordingly, Greenspan's comments were largely built in to Treasury prices, which explains the fairly subdued price action this session.

"If and when (the Fed) raises rates, since it constitutes a change in direction, Greenspan will feel compelled to convey some clear warning signs if such a move is coming," said Douglas Schindewolf, money market economist at Smith Barney Inc. "Today provided an obvious platform, but his testimony fell short of the clear warning signals he'll want to give if a rate hike is coming."
Schindewolf said that while there is still a bias toward tightening, a move in the near term is unlikely, with his forecast calling for no interest rate moves in 1997.

"What is lacking is higher wages being passed through, and that is a primary reason the Fed is able to stay on the sidelines," he said. "Given that the real federal funds rate is already relatively high, the current policy stance is already restrictive, so the risk of the Fed falling behind the inflation curve is pretty small."
Greenspan, though, suggested that it is only a matter of time before wage pressures spill over to consumer prices.
As such, some expect the Fed to raise rates in 1997, but not by more than 50 to 75 basis points.

"Greenspan said he was ready to tighten, but that there was no sense of urgency," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "He made it clear that he was preparing markets for a possible tightening move, but that he is also waiting for pressures in labor markets to affect (consumer) consumer products. So, it is too early to expect a tightening at the next (Fed) meeting February 4th and 5th." (( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
